concrete.simple: Solid, real, and specific enough that a reader can picture or test it.
concrete.detailed: Based on actual facts, objects, or examples rather than vague ideas; in school writing it means a claim you can point to, measure, or show.
concrete.example: The marker wanted concrete evidence, not a vague claim that 'the test went well'.
concrete.basic: The marker wanted real, specific evidence, not a vague claim.

conditional.simple: True only if another rule, fact, or event happens first.
conditional.detailed: Depending on a stated condition: a result, offer, or sentence is allowed only when that condition is met, as in 'if…then' thinking.
conditional.zh: 有条件的；视情况而定的
conditional.example: Her scholarship place was conditional on keeping a high average in Year 6.
conditional.basic: She would get the place only if she kept a high average.

confident.simple: Sure of your ability, idea, or judgement without showing off.
confident.detailed: Calmly certain that you can handle a task or that a claim is sound; in writing it sounds assured rather than shaky or boastful.
confident.example: A confident opening sentence told the reader she already knew her main point.
confident.basic: Her opening sentence sounded sure of the main point.

confidential.simple: Private and meant to be kept secret from people who should not see it.
confidential.detailed: Restricted information shared only with trusted people, such as a teacher's notes, a family's details, or a sealed enquiry.
confidential.example: Student medical notes are confidential and must not be left on a shared laptop.
confidential.basic: Student medical notes are private and must not be left out.

conflicting.simple: Pulling in opposite directions so the facts or views do not agree.
conflicting.detailed: Clashing or inconsistent: two witnesses, results, or arguments cannot both be fully true without further checking.
conflicting.example: The two graphs gave conflicting results, so the class repeated the trial.
conflicting.basic: The two graphs did not agree, so the class repeated the trial.

conscious.simple: Aware of what you are doing, thinking, or feeling in that moment.
conscious.detailed: Knowing and noticing your thoughts, choices, or surroundings; a conscious decision is made on purpose, not by accident.
conscious.example: The narrator makes a conscious choice to hide the letter, which changes the whole plot.
conscious.basic: The narrator chooses on purpose to hide the letter.

consecutive.simple: Following one after another with no gap in the sequence.
consecutive.detailed: Happening in an unbroken row of days, trials, pages, or results; useful when a pattern only matters if it keeps repeating in order.
consecutive.example: It rained on five consecutive days, so the creek sample stayed unusually high.
consecutive.basic: It rained on five days in a row, so the creek sample stayed high.

consequent.simple: Happening as a result of something that came before.
consequent.detailed: Following from an earlier cause: the later change, cost, or effect is explained by that first event, not by chance.
consequent.zh: 随之而来的；作为结果的
consequent.example: The dam failed, and the consequent flooding closed every road into town.
consequent.basic: The dam failed, and the flooding that followed closed the roads.

conservative.simple: Cautious about change, or careful not to overstate a result.
conservative.detailed: Preferring familiar ideas, low-risk estimates, or traditional practices; in data work a conservative figure is safely on the careful side.
conservative.example: We used a conservative estimate of 20 birds so we would not exaggerate the count.
conservative.basic: We used a careful, low estimate of 20 birds so we would not exaggerate.

considerate.simple: Thoughtful about other people's feelings, needs, or time.
considerate.detailed: Showing care by noticing how your words or actions affect others; in narrative it marks a character who thinks before they hurt someone.
considerate.example: A considerate teammate waited so the new student could finish her sentence.
considerate.basic: A kind teammate waited so the new student could finish speaking.

constitutional.simple: Allowed or required by a country's highest set of rules.
constitutional.detailed: Relating to a constitution: powers, rights, or limits that come from that founding law rather than from everyday habit.
constitutional.example: Freedom of speech is treated as a constitutional right in many democracies.
constitutional.basic: Freedom of speech is treated as a basic legal right in many democracies.

constructive.simple: Helpful because it improves a plan, idea, or piece of work.
constructive.detailed: Aimed at building something better: feedback, criticism, or action that points to a fix rather than only tearing a claim down.
constructive.example: Constructive criticism named one weak paragraph and suggested a clearer topic sentence.
constructive.basic: Helpful criticism named one weak paragraph and suggested a clearer start.

contemporary.simple: Belonging to the present time, or living in the same period.
contemporary.detailed: Modern, or existing at the same historical moment as something else; useful when you contrast today's practice with an older one.
contemporary.example: The HASS unit compared Federation speeches with contemporary news reports.
contemporary.basic: The HASS unit compared Federation speeches with news reports from the same time.

continual.simple: Happening again and again, often with short breaks in between.
continual.detailed: Repeated over time rather than one long unbroken stretch; continual interruptions keep starting, pausing, then starting again.
continual.zh: 频繁不断的；一再发生的
continual.example: Continual interruptions made it hard to finish the inquiry in one sitting.
continual.basic: Repeated interruptions made it hard to finish the inquiry.

continuous.simple: Going on without a break, pause, or gap in time or space.
continuous.detailed: Unbroken in time or space: a continuous line, sound, or process does not stop and restart the way a repeated event does.
continuous.example: The sensor recorded a continuous rise in temperature from dawn until noon.
continuous.basic: The sensor recorded a rise in temperature that did not stop from dawn until noon.

controversial.simple: Likely to cause strong disagreement because people see it very differently.
controversial.detailed: Disputed in public debate: a plan, text, or history topic that honest people argue about, so you must handle evidence fairly.
controversial.example: The new freeway was controversial because some families would lose parkland.
controversial.basic: The new freeway caused strong disagreement because some families would lose parkland.

convenient.simple: Easy to use, reach, or fit into your time without much trouble.
convenient.detailed: Suited to purpose because it saves effort, travel, or fuss; a convenient choice is practical, though it may not be the fairest one.
convenient.example: The library's evening hours were convenient for students who trained after school.
convenient.basic: The library's evening hours were easy to use for students who trained after school.

conventional.simple: Following the usual method, custom, or accepted way of doing things.
conventional.detailed: Standard or traditional rather than experimental; conventional wisdom is what most people already accept until new evidence arrives.
conventional.example: The class first tried the conventional method, then designed a fairer test of their own.
conventional.basic: The class first tried the usual method, then designed a fairer test.

convincing.simple: Strong enough in reason or evidence to make a fair reader believe it.
convincing.detailed: Persuasive because the proof, example, or voice is solid; a convincing argument does more than sound confident.
convincing.example: A convincing argument used two graphs and a clear counter-argument, not just slogans.
convincing.basic: A strong argument used two graphs and answered the other side, not just slogans.

cooperative.simple: Willing to work with others towards a shared goal.
cooperative.detailed: Helpful in a group: sharing tasks, listening, and combining effort so the class, team, or community can finish the job.
cooperative.example: A cooperative group finished the HASS poster because each person took one role.
cooperative.basic: A group that worked well together finished the poster because each person took a role.

core.simple: Most important or central to an idea, subject, or plan.
core.detailed: At the heart of a topic: core skills, core values, or a core claim are the parts you cannot drop without losing the main meaning.
core.example: The core idea of her essay was that fair rules protect the weakest players.
core.basic: The main idea of her essay was that fair rules protect the weakest players.

corporate.simple: Relating to a company or large business organisation.
corporate.detailed: Belonging to a corporation: its money, image, rules, or power, often discussed in HASS when businesses influence a community.
corporate.example: The council asked whether a corporate sponsor should put a logo on the community oval.
corporate.basic: The council asked whether a company sponsor should put a logo on the oval.

correct.simple: Free from mistakes, or matching the true facts and the required method.
correct.detailed: Accurate and proper: a correct answer, spelling, or procedure fits the evidence and the accepted rule, not just a lucky guess.
correct.example: The correct method was to measure three trials and then find the mean.
correct.basic: The right method was to measure three trials and then find the mean.

corresponding.simple: Matching another item in the same position, role, or amount.
corresponding.detailed: Paired or equivalent: a corresponding figure, year, or group lines up with the first one so you can compare them fairly.
corresponding.example: Each city on the map has a corresponding temperature on the table beside it.
corresponding.basic: Each city on the map has a matching temperature on the table beside it.

costly.simple: Expensive in money, time, or harmful results.
costly.detailed: Coming at a high price: a costly error, delay, or policy uses up resources or causes damage that is hard to reverse.
costly.example: A costly delay in fixing the leak wasted thousands of litres of water.
costly.basic: An expensive delay in fixing the leak wasted thousands of litres of water.

counterfeit.simple: Made as a fake copy meant to trick people into thinking it is real.
counterfeit.detailed: Forged or imitation, especially money, goods, or documents created to deceive; a counterfeit item has no honest value.
counterfeit.example: The museum displayed a counterfeit coin next to the genuine Federation piece.
counterfeit.basic: The museum displayed a fake coin next to the real Federation piece.

courageous.simple: Brave enough to do what is right even when it is frightening.
courageous.detailed: Showing courage in action or speech: a courageous character faces risk, unfairness, or shame rather than staying safely silent.
courageous.example: The courageous witness told the truth even though older students tried to silence her.
courageous.basic: The brave witness told the truth even though older students tried to silence her.

creative.simple: Able to invent fresh ideas, images, or solutions that are not copied.
creative.detailed: Original and imaginative in making or problem-solving; creative work still needs craft, not only wild guesses.
creative.example: A creative opening image made the drought feel close without using the word 'sad'.
creative.basic: An original opening image made the drought feel close without using the word 'sad'.

critical.simple: Carefully judging ideas, or so important that the result depends on it.
critical.detailed: In argument, critical thinking tests claims instead of accepting them; it can also mean a point that is vital to success or safety.
critical.example: Critical thinking asked whether the advertisement left out the product's real cost.
critical.basic: Careful judging asked whether the advertisement left out the real cost.

crucial.simple: Extremely important because the whole result can turn on it.
crucial.detailed: Decisive for success or failure: a crucial piece of evidence, step, or decision cannot be skipped if the argument or experiment is to hold.
crucial.example: The photograph was crucial evidence that the creek had overflowed overnight.
crucial.basic: The photograph was the key evidence that the creek had overflowed overnight.

crude.simple: Rough, unfinished, or in a raw form before it is refined.
crude.detailed: In science, crude can mean unprocessed material (such as crude oil) or a first, inexact measurement that still needs a finer method.
crude.example: A crude estimate of rainfall was enough to plan the first trial, but not the report.
crude.basic: A rough estimate of rainfall was enough to plan the first trial, but not the report.

cruel.simple: Willing to cause pain or take pleasure in someone else's suffering.
cruel.detailed: Harsh and unkind in a way that ignores another person's hurt; in literature it often reveals a character's abuse of power.
cruel.example: The cruel captain punished the cabin boy for a mistake he had not made.
cruel.basic: The harsh captain punished the cabin boy for a mistake he had not made.

cumulative.simple: Growing by adding more and more over time.
cumulative.detailed: Built from many small amounts stacked together: a cumulative total, effect, or error becomes large only after repeated additions.
cumulative.example: The cumulative effect of tiny leaks was a tank that emptied before Friday.
cumulative.basic: The added-up effect of tiny leaks was a tank that emptied before Friday.

cunning.simple: Clever in a sly way, often to trick someone or win an advantage.
cunning.detailed: Skilful and crafty: a cunning plan uses intelligence, but it may also hide a dishonest purpose, which readers should notice.
cunning.example: The cunning fox in the fable flatters the crow only to steal the cheese.
cunning.basic: The sly fox in the fable flatters the crow only to steal the cheese.

curious.simple: Eager to find out more, or strange enough to make you wonder.
curious.detailed: In literary work, curious usually marks a mind that asks questions; it can also describe an odd detail that invites closer reading.
curious.example: A curious reader notices why the author repeats the locked-gate image.
curious.basic: An eager reader notices why the author repeats the locked-gate image.

customary.simple: Usual because it is the accepted habit of a group or place.
customary.detailed: Following custom: a customary greeting, rule, or ceremony is what people in that community normally do, even if it is unwritten.
customary.example: It is customary in that community to welcome guests with a shared meal.
customary.basic: It is the usual habit in that community to welcome guests with a shared meal.

cynical.simple: Unwilling to trust people's good motives; expecting selfishness.
cynical.detailed: Doubtful that claims, leaders, or promises are sincere; a cynical voice can protect you from slogans, but it can also dismiss real care.
cynical.zh: 愤世嫉俗的；怀疑他人动机的
cynical.example: His cynical remark assumed the charity concert was only a publicity stunt.
cynical.basic: His distrustful remark assumed the charity concert was only for show.

damp.simple: Slightly wet; holding a little moisture but not soaked.
damp.detailed: In science, damp air, soil, or fabric contains water vapour or moisture that can change temperature, rust, mould, or plant growth.
damp.example: Seeds in damp soil sprouted two days earlier than seeds in the dry tray.
damp.basic: Seeds in slightly wet soil sprouted two days earlier than seeds in the dry tray.

dangerous.simple: Likely to cause harm, injury, or serious damage.
dangerous.detailed: Carrying a real risk to people, living things, or equipment; science writing names the hazard and the safe method, not just a scare word.
dangerous.example: The teacher labelled the dangerous chemical and kept it in a locked cabinet.
dangerous.basic: The teacher labelled the harmful chemical and kept it in a locked cabinet.

daring.simple: Bold enough to take a risk that others might avoid.
daring.detailed: Adventurous in action or style: a daring rescue, idea, or narrative choice pushes past the safe option, for better or worse.
daring.example: The daring rescue across the flooded causeway became the climax of the story.
daring.basic: The bold rescue across the flooded causeway became the climax of the story.

decisive.simple: Able to choose firmly, or able to settle a contest or argument.
decisive.detailed: Ending uncertainty: a decisive leader picks a path; a decisive piece of evidence is strong enough to decide the case.
decisive.example: One decisive graph settled the debate about which filter cleaned the water faster.
decisive.basic: One clear graph settled the debate about which filter cleaned the water faster.

decorative.simple: Made to look attractive rather than to do a practical job.
decorative.detailed: Ornamental: a decorative border, font, or object adds beauty or style, but it may carry little extra meaning or use.
decorative.example: The gold leaves on the title page were decorative and did not change the poem's meaning.
decorative.basic: The gold leaves on the title page were only for looks and did not change the meaning.

dedicated.simple: Giving steady time and care to a person, task, or cause.
dedicated.detailed: Committed with purpose: a dedicated volunteer, scientist, or chapter stays loyal to the work even when it is slow or hard.
dedicated.example: A dedicated volunteer watered the native seedlings every morning before school.
dedicated.basic: A committed volunteer watered the native seedlings every morning before school.

defensive.simple: Ready to protect yourself, a goal, or a claim from attack.
defensive.detailed: Guarding against harm or criticism: a defensive wall, team, or tone tries to stop a threat, sometimes instead of answering fairly.
defensive.example: His defensive tone appeared when the panel asked for the missing raw data.
defensive.basic: His guarded tone appeared when the panel asked for the missing raw data.

deliberate.simple: Done on purpose, or slow and careful rather than rushed.
deliberate.detailed: Intentional and considered: a deliberate choice is not an accident; a deliberate pace gives time to weigh evidence before you act.
deliberate.example: The author makes a deliberate pause before the last line so the secret can land.
deliberate.basic: The author makes a planned pause before the last line so the secret can land.

delicate.simple: Easily damaged, or needing gentle, precise handling.
delicate.detailed: Fine and fragile in body, feeling, or craft: a delicate instrument, ecosystem, or topic can be harmed by rough words or force.
delicate.example: The wetland was a delicate balance of salt and fresh water after the drought.
delicate.basic: The wetland was a fragile balance of salt and fresh water after the drought.

dense.simple: Packed tightly together, or hard to see through or read quickly.
dense.detailed: In science, dense matter has a lot of mass in a small space; in writing, a dense paragraph is packed with ideas and may need unpacking.
dense.example: The rainforest sample was so dense that almost no sunlight reached the litter.
dense.basic: The rainforest sample was so tightly packed that almost no sunlight reached the litter.

dependent.simple: Needing something or someone else in order to work or survive.
dependent.detailed: Reliant on another factor: a plant may be dependent on rainfall, or a result may be dependent on the variable you change.
dependent.example: Coral is dependent on clear, warm water, so muddy runoff is a serious threat.
dependent.basic: Coral needs clear, warm water, so muddy runoff is a serious threat.

descriptive.simple: Using details that help a reader picture a person, place, or thing.
descriptive.detailed: Focused on showing qualities through sensory or precise language rather than only telling a judgement; common in narrative and reports.
descriptive.example: A descriptive paragraph made the deserted jetty smell of salt and rust.
descriptive.basic: A detailed paragraph made the deserted jetty smell of salt and rust.

desirable.simple: Worth wanting because it is useful, fair, or attractive.
desirable.detailed: Judged as a good outcome: a desirable result, skill, or habitat is one people or living systems would benefit from having.
desirable.example: A desirable outcome was a cleaner creek and a safer swimming hole by summer.
desirable.basic: A worthwhile outcome was a cleaner creek and a safer swimming hole by summer.

desperate.simple: So worried or hopeless that you will try almost anything.
desperate.detailed: Driven by urgent need or despair: a desperate character takes risky action because ordinary choices no longer seem enough.
desperate.example: In a desperate attempt to save the farm, the family carted water through the night.
desperate.basic: In a last, frantic attempt to save the farm, the family carted water through the night.

destructive.simple: Causing serious damage or tearing things apart.
destructive.detailed: Harmful to structures, habitats, or relationships: a destructive storm, habit, or argument leaves wreckage rather than a better plan.
destructive.example: The destructive storm flattened the dune fence and washed sand across the road.
destructive.basic: The damaging storm flattened the dune fence and washed sand across the road.

detrimental.simple: Causing harm or making a situation worse.
detrimental.detailed: Having a damaging effect on health, learning, habitat, or fairness, even when the harm is slow or not immediately obvious.
detrimental.example: Late-night phone use can be detrimental to sleep and next-day concentration.
detrimental.basic: Late-night phone use can be harmful to sleep and next-day concentration.

devoted.simple: Deeply loyal and willing to give time and care to someone or something.
devoted.detailed: Lovingly committed: a devoted friend, carer, or cause receives steady attention, which literature often contrasts with neglect.
devoted.example: The devoted older sister packed lunch and notes even after a long night shift.
devoted.basic: The loyal older sister packed lunch and notes even after a long night shift.

diplomatic.simple: Careful and polite when dealing with people who may disagree.
diplomatic.detailed: Skilled at keeping peace between sides; in HASS it also means relating to official talks between countries or communities.
diplomatic.example: A diplomatic answer praised both teams before naming the one rule that had to change.
diplomatic.basic: A careful, polite answer praised both teams before naming the one rule that had to change.

direct.simple: Straight, clear, and without extra steps or hidden meaning.
direct.detailed: Going by the shortest honest path: a direct route, question, or style does not dodge the point or hide behind extra words.
direct.example: A direct question asked who had changed the data, and the room went quiet.
direct.basic: A straight question asked who had changed the data, and the room went quiet.

disadvantaged.simple: Having fewer chances, resources, or supports than other people.
disadvantaged.detailed: Held back by unfair conditions such as poverty, distance, or discrimination; HASS writing names the barrier rather than blaming the person.
disadvantaged.zh: 处于不利地位的；弱势的
disadvantaged.example: The grant targeted disadvantaged students who had no quiet place to study at home.
disadvantaged.basic: The grant targeted students who had fewer chances and no quiet place to study.

disappointed.simple: Sad or let down because something was not as good as you hoped.
disappointed.detailed: Feeling the gap between hope and result; in narrative it often turns a character towards a new choice rather than only a sulk.
disappointed.example: She looked disappointed when the scholarship shortlist left out her closest friend.
disappointed.basic: She looked let down when the scholarship shortlist left out her closest friend.

disastrous.simple: Causing great damage, failure, or suffering.
disastrous.detailed: So harmful that recovery is hard: a disastrous flood, plan, or decision wrecks homes, trust, or a carefully built project.
disastrous.example: A disastrous flood washed away the footbridge and cut the town off for a week.
disastrous.basic: A terrible flood washed away the footbridge and cut the town off for a week.

disciplinary.simple: Connected with rules, training, or punishment for breaking them.
disciplinary.detailed: About keeping order and standards: a disciplinary meeting, policy, or action responds to misconduct and tries to teach a fairer habit.
disciplinary.example: The principal called a disciplinary meeting after the copied assignment was found.
disciplinary.basic: The principal called a rules-and-consequences meeting after the copied assignment was found.

abolish.simple: To officially end a law, rule, or system so it no longer exists.
abolish.detailed: To cancel something by authority: parliament, a council, or a school can abolish a practice that is judged unfair or outdated.
abolish.example: The council voted to abolish the outdated rule that banned bikes from the oval.
abolish.basic: The council voted to end the outdated rule that banned bikes from the oval.

accentuate.simple: To make a feature stand out more clearly so people notice it.
accentuate.detailed: To highlight a quality, contrast, or image on purpose, often in writing or design, so the important part is impossible to miss.
accentuate.example: Short, sharp sentences accentuate the panic as the river bursts its banks.
accentuate.basic: Short, sharp sentences make the panic stand out as the river bursts its banks.

acquiesce.simple: To go along with a plan even if you are not keen on it.
acquiesce.detailed: To accept something quietly, without a real fight, often because arguing seems useless or because you want peace more than victory.
acquiesce.example: The class did not want extra drills, but they still acquiesce when the scholarship date is explained.
acquiesce.basic: The class does not want extra drills, but they still go along when the date is explained.

adjudicate.simple: To judge a dispute or contest and give an official decision.
adjudicate.detailed: To hear both sides and settle who is right, who wins, or what the rule requires, as a referee, panel, or court would do.
adjudicate.example: An independent teacher will adjudicate the debate so neither house marks its own team.
adjudicate.basic: An independent teacher will judge the debate so neither house marks its own team.

alleviate.simple: To make pain, pressure, or a problem less severe.
alleviate.detailed: To reduce harm without always removing the cause: shade can alleviate heat stress, and a fair plan can alleviate crowding.
alleviate.example: Planting shade trees can alleviate heat stress for students waiting at the bus stop.
alleviate.basic: Planting shade trees can ease heat stress for students waiting at the bus stop.

amalgamate.simple: To join two or more groups or things into one larger whole.
amalgamate.detailed: To merge organisations, classes, or materials so they operate as a single unit, often to share resources or simplify a system.
amalgamate.example: The two small libraries will amalgamate next term so one catalogue serves the whole town.
amalgamate.basic: The two small libraries will join into one next term so one catalogue serves the town.

ameliorate.simple: To make a bad situation a little better.
ameliorate.detailed: To improve conditions that are already poor: extra tutors, cleaner water, or a fairer rule can ameliorate harm even if the problem is not gone.
ameliorate.example: Extra reading tutors helped ameliorate the gap for students who had missed a term.
ameliorate.basic: Extra reading tutors helped make the gap a little better for students who had missed a term.

appease.simple: To calm someone by giving in a little so the conflict eases.
appease.detailed: To soothe anger or demand, sometimes by a compromise that keeps peace in the short term but may not solve the real issue.
appease.example: The mayor tried to appease angry residents by delaying the freeway vote for a month.
appease.basic: The mayor tried to calm angry residents by delaying the freeway vote for a month.

ascribe.simple: To say that a result or quality comes from a particular cause or person.
ascribe.detailed: To attribute something: you ascribe a win to practice, a drought to climate patterns, or a quotation to its real author.
ascribe.example: Do not ascribe the whole score drop to one test if three other factors also changed.
ascribe.basic: Do not blame the whole score drop on one test if three other factors also changed.

attenuate.simple: To weaken a force, signal, or effect so it is less strong.
attenuate.detailed: To reduce intensity: distance can attenuate sound, a filter can attenuate light, and careful wording can attenuate a harsh claim.
attenuate.example: Thick fog can attenuate the lighthouse beam so ships see it only at close range.
attenuate.basic: Thick fog can weaken the lighthouse beam so ships see it only at close range.

augment.simple: To add to something so it becomes larger or stronger.
augment.detailed: To increase by adding extra support: extra data can augment a report, and extra practice can augment a skill you already have.
augment.example: Two more trials will augment the data set before we write the conclusion.
augment.basic: Two more trials will add to the data set before we write the conclusion.

bolster.simple: To support or strengthen an idea, person, or structure.
bolster.detailed: To prop something up so it holds: extra evidence can bolster a claim, and encouragement can bolster a teammate's confidence.
bolster.example: A second graph will bolster the claim that the filter actually works.
bolster.basic: A second graph will support the claim that the filter actually works.

capitulate.simple: To give in and stop resisting after a struggle.
capitulate.detailed: To surrender a fight, argument, or demand, usually because continuing no longer seems possible or worth the cost.
capitulate.example: The strikers refused to capitulate until the unsafe machines were replaced.
capitulate.basic: The strikers refused to give in until the unsafe machines were replaced.

circumvent.simple: To get around a rule or obstacle instead of meeting it head-on.
circumvent.detailed: To avoid a barrier by finding another path: some students try to circumvent a word limit, and engineers circumvent a blocked road.
circumvent.example: Honest writers do not circumvent the word limit by shrinking the font.
circumvent.basic: Honest writers do not dodge the word limit by shrinking the font.

coalesce.simple: To come together and form one group, mass, or idea.
coalesce.detailed: To merge from separate parts: droplets can coalesce into a drop, and scattered clues can coalesce into one explanation.
coalesce.example: Tiny oil droplets coalesce into one shiny layer on the surface of the beaker.
coalesce.basic: Tiny oil droplets join together into one shiny layer on the surface of the beaker.

collate.simple: To gather pages or facts and put them in a useful order.
collate.detailed: To collect and arrange information from more than one place so you can compare it fairly before you write or decide.
collate.example: Please collate the three trial sheets before you calculate the class mean.
collate.basic: Please gather and order the three trial sheets before you calculate the mean.

conjecture.simple: To suggest an idea that might be true when you do not yet have proof.
conjecture.detailed: To form a reasoned guess from incomplete clues; a conjecture is useful for planning the next test, but it is not a finished conclusion.
conjecture.example: We can conjecture that the plants failed from salt, but we still need a soil test.
conjecture.basic: We can guess that the plants failed from salt, but we still need a soil test.

consolidate.simple: To make something stronger or more organised by bringing parts together.
consolidate.detailed: To firm up gains: a class can consolidate skills through review, and a council can consolidate two offices into one clearer system.
consolidate.example: Friday's lesson will consolidate the week's grammar so it sticks for the test.
consolidate.basic: Friday's lesson will strengthen and organise the week's grammar so it sticks.

construe.simple: To understand words or actions as having a particular meaning.
construe.detailed: To interpret: the same remark can be construed as a joke or an insult, so careful readers check context before they judge.
construe.example: Some readers construe the last line as hope; others hear only warning.
construe.basic: Some readers take the last line as hope; others hear only warning.

counteract.simple: To work against an effect so it becomes weaker or cancelled.
counteract.detailed: To oppose a force with another force: lime can counteract acidity, and a fair rule can counteract an unfair advantage.
counteract.example: A pinch of baking soda can counteract the acidity of the vinegar in this test.
counteract.basic: A pinch of baking soda can cancel the acidity of the vinegar in this test.

curtail.simple: To cut something back so it lasts a shorter time or has a smaller range.
curtail.detailed: To limit or shorten by authority or necessity: a drought can curtail watering, and a new law can curtail an unsafe practice.
curtail.example: The drought forced the council to curtail watering of public lawns.
curtail.basic: The drought forced the council to cut back watering of public lawns.

decipher.simple: To work out the meaning of something that is hard to read or understand.
decipher.detailed: To decode messy writing, a code, or a puzzling scene so the hidden message becomes clear enough to use.
decipher.example: It took the class ten minutes to decipher the faded diary entry from 1901.
decipher.basic: It took the class ten minutes to work out the faded diary entry from 1901.

delineate.simple: To show the shape or limits of something in a clear, careful way.
delineate.detailed: To draw or describe boundaries and parts so a reader can see how a plan, character, or region is organised.
delineate.example: The map must delineate the flood zone so families know which streets are at risk.
delineate.basic: The map must show the flood zone clearly so families know which streets are at risk.

demolish.simple: To knock a building or argument down so little of it is left.
demolish.detailed: To destroy a structure, or to wreck a claim with evidence so strong that the old position cannot stand.
demolish.example: New census figures demolish the claim that the town is still shrinking.
demolish.basic: New census figures wreck the claim that the town is still shrinking.

deplete.simple: To use up a supply until little or nothing remains.
deplete.detailed: To drain a resource: overfishing can deplete a species, and long droughts can deplete stored water in a dam.
deplete.example: Overwatering can deplete nutrients in the potting mix and weaken the seedlings.
deplete.basic: Overwatering can use up nutrients in the potting mix and weaken the seedlings.

deplore.simple: To say strongly that something is wrong and that you regret it.
deplore.detailed: To condemn a harmful act or situation in public language: you deplore cruelty, waste, or unfair treatment rather than shrugging it off.
deplore.example: The editorial will deplore the dumping of rubbish in the protected wetland.
deplore.basic: The editorial will say the dumping of rubbish in the wetland is wrong.

deride.simple: To laugh at someone or something as if it were foolish or worthless.
deride.detailed: To mock in a scornful way: a character who derides a classmate's idea tries to shrink it, which readers should treat as unfair attack.
deride.example: It is cheap to deride a first draft instead of naming one change that would help.
deride.basic: It is cheap to laugh at a first draft instead of naming one change that would help.

disseminate.simple: To spread information widely so many people can use it.
disseminate.detailed: To circulate findings, warnings, or ideas through talks, posters, or publications so they leave one classroom or lab and reach others.
disseminate.example: The science club will disseminate its water-quality findings at Saturday's market.
disseminate.basic: The science club will spread its water-quality findings at Saturday's market.

divulge.simple: To tell a secret or private fact that was meant to stay hidden.
divulge.detailed: To reveal confidential information, sometimes by accident and sometimes on purpose; once divulged, the fact cannot be taken back.
divulge.example: The diary does not divulge the thief's name until the final chapter.
divulge.basic: The diary does not tell the thief's name until the final chapter.

elucidate.simple: To explain something clearly so it is no longer confusing.
elucidate.detailed: To throw light on a hard idea with examples, steps, or simpler wording until a reader can follow the reasoning.
elucidate.example: A labelled diagram will elucidate the water cycle better than a dense paragraph.
elucidate.basic: A labelled diagram will make the water cycle clearer than a dense paragraph.

emanate.simple: To come out from a source, as light, smell, or a feeling does.
emanate.detailed: To flow or radiate outward: heat can emanate from rocks, and tension can emanate from a silent character in a scene.
emanate.example: A faint smell of smoke began to emanate from the sealed science storeroom.
emanate.basic: A faint smell of smoke began to come out of the sealed science storeroom.

emulate.simple: To copy a person or model because you want to match their standard.
emulate.detailed: To imitate with respect and effort: students may emulate a writer's craft, and engineers may emulate a design that already works.
emulate.example: Young poets often emulate Banjo Paterson's galloping rhythm before finding their own.
emulate.basic: Young poets often copy Banjo Paterson's galloping rhythm before finding their own.

engender.simple: To cause a feeling, idea, or situation to start.
engender.detailed: To give rise to something, especially an attitude or result: unfair rules can engender resentment, and praise can engender trust.
engender.example: Clear marking comments can engender trust that the grade was fairly earned.
engender.basic: Clear marking comments can create trust that the grade was fairly earned.

enthral.simple: To hold someone's full attention as if they cannot look away.
enthral.detailed: To fascinate: a story, speaker, or performance can enthral an audience so completely that time seems to disappear.
enthral.example: The visiting storyteller could enthral a restless Year 6 class in under a minute.
enthral.basic: The visiting storyteller could hold a restless Year 6 class in under a minute.

enumerate.simple: To list items one by one so none is missed.
enumerate.detailed: To count or name each part in order: a report may enumerate reasons, steps, or species so the set is complete and checkable.
enumerate.example: Please enumerate the three variables you changed so the method can be repeated.
enumerate.basic: Please list the three variables you changed so the method can be repeated.

epitomise.simple: To be a perfect, typical example of a quality or idea.
epitomise.detailed: To stand as the clearest case: one scene, person, or object can epitomise a whole theme, which is useful in literary analysis.
epitomise.example: The cracked water tank seems to epitomise the town's long struggle with drought.
epitomise.basic: The cracked water tank seems to be the perfect example of the town's struggle with drought.

eradicate.simple: To remove something harmful completely so it does not return.
eradicate.detailed: To wipe out a pest, disease, or practice: quarantine and careful work can eradicate weeds, but the word promises a thorough job.
eradicate.example: Rangers hope to eradicate the invasive vine before it reaches the national park.
eradicate.basic: Rangers hope to wipe out the invasive vine before it reaches the national park.

espouse.simple: To support an idea or cause openly and stand by it.
espouse.detailed: To adopt a view as your own and argue for it: a speaker may espouse fairness, a party may espouse a policy, and you should test the reasons.
espouse.example: The candidate will espouse a ban on single-use plastics in the harbour.
espouse.basic: The candidate will openly support a ban on single-use plastics in the harbour.

evade.simple: To escape or dodge something you do not want to face.
evade.detailed: To avoid capture, a question, or a duty by slipping aside: a character may evade the truth, which often becomes part of the plot.
evade.example: The narrator tries to evade the question about the missing key for two whole chapters.
evade.basic: The narrator tries to dodge the question about the missing key for two whole chapters.

evince.simple: To show a quality or feeling clearly through words or actions.
evince.detailed: To make something evident: a calm reply can evince patience, and a data table can evince a pattern you then explain.
evince.example: Her careful footnotes evince a respect for other people's research.
evince.basic: Her careful footnotes show a respect for other people's research.

exalt.simple: To praise someone or something as if they were unusually high or noble.
exalt.detailed: To lift up in honour: a poem may exalt a hero, and a speech may exalt a value; readers should ask whether the praise is earned.
exalt.example: The anthem seems to exalt the explorers and barely mentions the people already living there.
exalt.basic: The anthem seems to praise the explorers and barely mentions the people already living there.

exasperate.simple: To annoy someone so much that they lose patience.
exasperate.detailed: To frustrate again and again until calm breaks: a delay, a tease, or a stubborn rule can exasperate even a careful character.
exasperate.example: The broken printer will exasperate the team if the posters are due at three.
exasperate.basic: The broken printer will drive the team mad if the posters are due at three.

exemplify.simple: To show a rule or idea by giving a clear example of it.
exemplify.detailed: To stand as a typical case, or to illustrate a point with one well-chosen instance so the abstract idea becomes concrete.
exemplify.example: This one creek sample can exemplify the wider problem of farm runoff.
exemplify.basic: This one creek sample can stand as a clear example of the wider runoff problem.

expedite.simple: To make a process happen faster without skipping the necessary steps.
expedite.detailed: To speed up official or practical work: extra staff can expedite marking, and a clear form can expedite a permission request.
expedite.example: A complete permission form will expedite the excursion approval this week.
expedite.basic: A complete permission form will speed up the excursion approval this week.

extol.simple: To praise someone or something in strong, open language.
extol.detailed: To speak highly and at length: a review may extol a book, and a speech may extol a community's courage after a disaster.
extol.example: The review will extol the novel's humour without hiding its uneven ending.
extol.basic: The review will praise the novel's humour without hiding its uneven ending.

extrapolate.simple: To estimate what will happen next by extending a pattern you already see.
extrapolate.detailed: To project beyond measured points: from two years of data you may extrapolate a third, but you must say the extra year is an estimate.
extrapolate.example: We can extrapolate next month's rainfall only if the last five years follow a stable pattern.
extrapolate.basic: We can estimate next month's rainfall only if the last five years follow a stable pattern.

fabricate.simple: To invent a story or piece of evidence that is not true.
fabricate.detailed: To make something up, especially a lie or fake proof; in argument it is a serious fault because fabricated evidence destroys trust.
fabricate.example: Do not fabricate data in a science log, or you will have to repeat the whole investigation.
fabricate.basic: Do not invent data in a science log, or you will have to repeat the whole investigation.

galvanise.simple: To shock or inspire people so they suddenly take action.
galvanise.detailed: To stir a group into energy: a speech, crisis, or unfair rule can galvanise a community that had been slow to move.
galvanise.example: Photos of the dying reef helped galvanise the town into a weekend clean-up.
galvanise.basic: Photos of the dying reef helped stir the town into a weekend clean-up.

impede.simple: To slow or block progress so something is harder to finish.
impede.detailed: To get in the way: mud can impede a walker, and missing data can impede a fair conclusion.
impede.example: Missing raw scores will impede any fair comparison between the two classes.
impede.basic: Missing raw scores will slow any fair comparison between the two classes.

incriminate.simple: To make someone look guilty of a wrong act.
incriminate.detailed: To provide evidence that points to blame: a fingerprint or a dishonest message can incriminate a person, so the proof must be handled fairly.
incriminate.example: The unsigned note seemed to incriminate the prefect, but the handwriting did not match.
incriminate.basic: The unsigned note seemed to make the prefect look guilty, but the handwriting did not match.

inculcate.simple: To teach a habit or belief by repeating it until it sticks.
inculcate.detailed: To fix an idea in someone's mind through steady practice: schools may inculcate honesty, and families may inculcate a daily reading habit.
inculcate.example: Morning reading time can inculcate a habit that lasts long after Year 6.
inculcate.basic: Morning reading time can teach a habit that lasts long after Year 6.

indemnify.simple: To promise to cover someone's loss, damage, or legal cost.
indemnify.detailed: To protect a person or group with a guarantee of payment if harm occurs, often written into a contract or insurance agreement.
indemnify.example: The hire form says the club must indemnify the council if the oval is damaged.
indemnify.basic: The hire form says the club must cover the council's loss if the oval is damaged.

instigate.simple: To start an action, especially a protest, plan, or piece of trouble.
instigate.detailed: To set something in motion, often by urging others: a student may instigate a petition, and a rumour can instigate a quarrel.
instigate.example: Two Year 6 captains helped instigate the petition for a safer crossing.
instigate.basic: Two Year 6 captains helped start the petition for a safer crossing.

interrogate.simple: To ask someone a series of serious, searching questions.
interrogate.detailed: To question closely, as police, historians, or careful readers do; you can also interrogate a source by testing what it leaves out.
interrogate.example: Good historians interrogate a source by asking who wrote it and what they wanted.
interrogate.basic: Good historians question a source closely by asking who wrote it and what they wanted.

lament.simple: To express sorrow or regret about a loss or a sad change.
lament.detailed: To mourn in words: a poem may lament a death, and a speech may lament a ruined habitat, mixing grief with a wish that things were otherwise.
lament.example: The final stanza will lament the last gum tree on the cleared ridge.
lament.basic: The final stanza will express sorrow for the last gum tree on the cleared ridge.

magnify.simple: To make something look larger, or to make a problem seem bigger.
magnify.detailed: To enlarge with a lens, or to increase the apparent size of an error, feeling, or effect so it is easier to notice (or easier to overstate).
magnify.example: A hand lens will magnify the leaf veins so the class can sketch them accurately.
magnify.basic: A hand lens will make the leaf veins look larger so the class can sketch them.

manifest.simple: To show a quality clearly, or to become obvious in what people can see.
manifest.detailed: To appear in a form others can notice: stress may manifest as headaches, and fairness can manifest in how a teacher shares time.
manifest.example: The same worry began to manifest as unfinished homework and short tempers.
manifest.basic: The same worry began to show up as unfinished homework and short tempers.

obfuscate.simple: To make an idea harder to understand, sometimes on purpose.
obfuscate.detailed: To cloud meaning with extra words, jargon, or missing steps so a reader cannot test the claim easily; the opposite of clarifying.
obfuscate.example: Long slogans can obfuscate the real cost of the plan instead of explaining it.
obfuscate.basic: Long slogans can hide the real cost of the plan instead of explaining it.

obviate.simple: To remove the need for something by dealing with the cause first.
obviate.detailed: To make a later step unnecessary: a clear rubric can obviate extra questions, and a vaccine can obviate a later outbreak in a community.
obviate.example: A labelled equipment list will obviate the need for last-minute shop runs.
obviate.basic: A labelled equipment list will remove the need for last-minute shop runs.

oscillate.simple: To swing back and forth between two positions, values, or ideas.
oscillate.detailed: To move repeatedly from one side to the other: a pendulum can oscillate, and a character's loyalty can oscillate between two friends.
oscillate.example: The compass needle will oscillate before it settles on magnetic north.
oscillate.basic: The compass needle will swing back and forth before it settles on magnetic north.

pervade.simple: To spread through every part of a place, group, or piece of writing.
pervade.detailed: To be present everywhere in a scene or mood: smoke can pervade a valley, and dread can pervade a chapter without one scare word.
pervade.example: A smell of wet wool seemed to pervade the hall after the storm.
pervade.basic: A smell of wet wool seemed to fill every part of the hall after the storm.

postulate.simple: To put forward an idea as a starting point that still needs testing.
postulate.detailed: To state an assumption you will work from: scientists postulate a cause, then design a trial; the postulate is not yet a proven law.
postulate.example: We postulate that salt, not heat, stunted the seedlings, and then we test each factor.
postulate.basic: We start from the idea that salt, not heat, stunted the seedlings, and then we test it.

precipitate.simple: To make a solid form in a liquid, or to cause an event to happen suddenly.
precipitate.detailed: In chemistry, a solid can precipitate from a solution; in wider science writing, a trigger can precipitate a rapid change such as a landslide.
precipitate.example: When the two clear solutions mixed, a white solid began to precipitate in the beaker.
precipitate.basic: When the two clear solutions mixed, a white solid began to form in the beaker.

preclude.simple: To make something impossible by blocking it in advance.
preclude.detailed: To shut a path before it opens: a missing permission note can preclude a student from the excursion, and one fact can preclude a weak theory.
preclude.example: A missing signature will preclude her from the overnight science camp.
preclude.basic: A missing signature will stop her from joining the overnight science camp.

presuppose.simple: To take something as already true before you start the next step.
presuppose.detailed: To depend on an unstated assumption: a test may presuppose that students know the method, so a fair paper makes that assumption visible.
presuppose.example: The worksheet seems to presuppose that every student has already seen a compass rose.
presuppose.basic: The worksheet seems to take it as already true that every student has seen a compass rose.

proliferate.simple: To increase quickly in number and spread more widely.
proliferate.detailed: To multiply and spread: algae can proliferate in warm water, and rumours can proliferate online if nobody checks them.
proliferate.example: Algae can proliferate in warm, still water and starve fish of oxygen.
proliferate.basic: Algae can increase quickly in warm, still water and starve fish of oxygen.

propound.simple: To put forward an idea carefully so others can consider it.
propound.detailed: To offer a theory or argument for discussion: a speaker may propound a solution, and the class then tests whether the reasons hold.
propound.example: In the final paragraph she will propound a simpler rule for sharing the courts.
propound.basic: In the final paragraph she will put forward a simpler rule for sharing the courts.

ratify.simple: To give formal approval so an agreement becomes official.
ratify.detailed: To confirm a treaty, constitution, or club rule by a vote or signature after it has already been drafted.
ratify.example: The student council must ratify the new constitution before it can take effect.
ratify.basic: The student council must formally approve the new constitution before it can take effect.

rebut.simple: To answer a claim with reasons or evidence that show it is weak.
rebut.detailed: To fight back in argument by pointing to facts that contradict the other side, not by insulting the speaker.
rebut.example: Use the second graph to rebut the claim that recycling made no difference.
rebut.basic: Use the second graph to answer the claim that recycling made no difference.

recant.simple: To take back a claim you made earlier and say it was wrong.
recant.detailed: To withdraw a statement, especially a strong public one, after new evidence or pressure; in argument it is a serious change of position.
recant.example: After the second trial he had to recant the claim that the filter never clogged.
recant.basic: After the second trial he had to take back the claim that the filter never clogged.

redress.simple: To put right a harm or unfair situation, often by making amends.
redress.detailed: To correct an injustice with action, payment, or a changed rule so the injured side is treated more fairly than before.
redress.example: The council promised to redress the unfair bus timetable for the outer suburbs.
redress.basic: The council promised to put right the unfair bus timetable for the outer suburbs.

repudiate.simple: To reject an idea, claim, or connection as untrue or unwanted.
repudiate.detailed: To refuse to accept or be associated with something: a leader may repudiate a rumour, and a writer may repudiate an old view.
repudiate.example: The captain will repudiate the rumour that the team cheated on the fitness test.
repudiate.basic: The captain will reject the rumour that the team cheated on the fitness test.

rescind.simple: To cancel an official decision, rule, or offer so it no longer applies.
rescind.detailed: To take back a legal or formal act: a council can rescind a ban, and a school can rescind a permission that was granted in error.
rescind.example: Parents asked the board to rescind the ban on homemade food at the fete.
rescind.basic: Parents asked the board to cancel the ban on homemade food at the fete.

substantiate.simple: To give solid evidence that shows a claim is true.
substantiate.detailed: To back a statement with facts, data, or reliable sources so it is no longer only an opinion.
substantiate.example: Two independent counts help substantiate the claim that bird numbers have risen.
substantiate.basic: Two independent counts help prove the claim that bird numbers have risen.

subvert.simple: To weaken a system, rule, or story from the inside so it no longer holds.
subvert.detailed: To undermine authority or an expected meaning: a satire can subvert a proud slogan, and a secret deal can subvert a fair vote.
subvert.example: The last chapter will subvert the hero myth by showing who really paid the cost.
subvert.basic: The last chapter will quietly overturn the hero myth by showing who really paid the cost.

surmise.simple: To form an idea from clues when you cannot be completely sure.
surmise.detailed: To infer a likely explanation from incomplete evidence; a surmise is smarter than a wild guess, but it still needs a check.
surmise.example: From the muddy prints we can surmise that the thief left after the storm began.
surmise.basic: From the muddy prints we can reasonably guess that the thief left after the storm began.

truncate.simple: To cut something short so the end is missing or shortened.
truncate.detailed: To shorten by chopping: a graph axis can be truncated, and a quotation can be truncated if you mark the missing words honestly.
truncate.example: Do not truncate the y-axis in a way that makes a tiny change look huge.
truncate.basic: Do not cut the y-axis short in a way that makes a tiny change look huge.

underscore.simple: To emphasise a point so a reader cannot miss its importance.
underscore.detailed: To stress a claim with words, evidence, or repetition; in argument it is a way of pointing, not a substitute for proof.
underscore.example: The final statistic will underscore the need for a safer crossing before summer.
underscore.basic: The final statistic will emphasise the need for a safer crossing before summer.

usurp.simple: To seize a role or power that rightfully belongs to someone else.
usurp.detailed: To take control without a fair claim: a character may usurp a throne, and a loud voice may usurp a meeting that others should lead.
usurp.example: In the play, the younger brother tries to usurp the farm that the will left to his sister.
usurp.basic: In the play, the younger brother tries to seize the farm that the will left to his sister.

vindicate.simple: To clear someone of blame, or to show that a criticised idea was right.
vindicate.detailed: To justify after doubt: later evidence can vindicate a student who was accused, or vindicate a method that others called wasteful.
vindicate.example: The second lab book helped vindicate the student who had been accused of inventing results.
vindicate.basic: The second lab book helped clear the student who had been accused of inventing results.

aberration.simple: A result or action that is not normal for the pattern you usually see.
aberration.detailed: A one-off departure from what is typical: a single extreme score can be an aberration, so scientists check before they change a whole theory.
aberration.example: One huge outlier may be an aberration caused by a misread thermometer.
aberration.basic: One huge outlier may be an unusual result caused by a misread thermometer.

accolade.simple: Public praise or an honour given for excellent work.
accolade.detailed: A formal compliment, prize, or title that recognises achievement; in writing it can also mean high praise from a critic or community.
accolade.example: Winning the state writing prize was the highest accolade the class had ever seen.
accolade.basic: Winning the state writing prize was the highest honour the class had ever seen.

acrimony.simple: Bitter, sharp unfriendliness in an argument or relationship.
acrimony.detailed: Angry hostility that makes discussion sour: acrimony in a council debate or a family scene shows that feelings have overtaken fair reasons.
acrimony.example: Acrimony between the two captains made a simple roster sound like a feud.
acrimony.basic: Bitter unfriendliness between the two captains made a simple roster sound like a feud.

adage.simple: A short traditional saying that offers a piece of common wisdom.
adage.detailed: A familiar proverb-like sentence people repeat as advice; useful in literary study when a character lives by an old saying, wisely or not.
adage.example: The coach repeated the old adage that slow practice beats rushed guessing.
adage.basic: The coach repeated the old saying that slow practice beats rushed guessing.

affinity.simple: A natural liking or close connection between people, ideas, or things.
affinity.detailed: A pull towards someone or something: a reader may feel affinity with a character, and two chemicals may show affinity in how they bond.
affinity.example: She felt an immediate affinity with the quiet narrator who also loved maps.
affinity.basic: She felt an immediate liking and connection with the quiet narrator who also loved maps.

aftermath.simple: The period and effects that follow a disaster, fight, or big event.
aftermath.detailed: What is left once the main shock is over: ruined fences, new laws, or changed feelings that a community must face after the crisis.
aftermath.example: In the aftermath of the flood, the school became a shelter for two weeks.
aftermath.basic: In the time after the flood, the school became a shelter for two weeks.

alacrity.simple: Cheerful quickness; being ready and willing to act at once.
alacrity.detailed: Lively eagerness rather than reluctant dragging: a character who accepts a task with alacrity shows energy and goodwill.
alacrity.example: The volunteers packed sandbags with alacrity when the creek warnings began.
alacrity.basic: The volunteers packed sandbags quickly and willingly when the creek warnings began.

allegory.simple: A story whose characters and events stand for deeper ideas.
allegory.detailed: A narrative that works on two levels: the surface plot and a second meaning about society, morals, or history that careful readers decode.
allegory.example: The animal farm story is an allegory of how power can corrupt a revolution.
allegory.basic: The animal farm story is a tale whose animals stand for how power can corrupt a revolution.

anachronism.simple: Something that does not belong in that time period.
anachronism.detailed: A detail placed in the wrong era, by mistake or on purpose: a digital watch in a 1901 scene is an anachronism that breaks or comments on the setting.
anachronism.zh: 时代错置；不合时代之物
anachronism.example: A plastic water bottle in the 1850s camp scene is an obvious anachronism.
anachronism.basic: A plastic water bottle in the 1850s camp scene clearly does not belong in that time.

anecdote.simple: A short true-sounding story used to illustrate a point.
anecdote.detailed: A brief personal or historical incident, often vivid; useful in speeches, but one anecdote is not enough proof for a wide claim.
anecdote.example: One funny anecdote about a lost compass made the safety talk easier to remember.
anecdote.basic: One short true-sounding story about a lost compass made the safety talk easier to remember.

antagonist.simple: The character or force that works against the main character.
antagonist.detailed: The opponent in a narrative: a person, group, or even a storm can be the antagonist that the protagonist must face.
antagonist.example: The river itself becomes the antagonist once the family is trapped on the island.
antagonist.basic: The river itself becomes the opposing force once the family is trapped on the island.

antithesis.simple: The exact opposite of an idea, person, or quality.
antithesis.detailed: A sharp contrast used in argument or style: one claim is set against its antithesis so the difference is unmistakable.
antithesis.example: His noisy showing-off was the antithesis of the quiet courage the novel praises.
antithesis.basic: His noisy showing-off was the exact opposite of the quiet courage the novel praises.

apathy.simple: A lack of interest, feeling, or willingness to act.
apathy.detailed: Emotional flatness or civic unconcern: apathy can let an unfair rule stand because nobody cares enough to challenge it.
apathy.example: Public apathy about the dying creek allowed the dumping to continue for years.
apathy.basic: Public lack of interest in the dying creek allowed the dumping to continue for years.

apex.simple: The highest point of a shape, career, or process.
apex.detailed: The peak or tip: a triangle has an apex, and a story or career can reach an apex just before things change again.
apex.example: The hawk is an apex predator in this woodland food web.
apex.basic: The hawk is the top predator in this woodland food web.

aphorism.simple: A short, memorable sentence that states a general truth or attitude.
aphorism.detailed: A compact, witty remark that sounds like wisdom; in literature it can reveal a character's values in a single line.
aphorism.example: The novel opens with an aphorism about luck favouring the prepared traveller.
aphorism.basic: The novel opens with a short, memorable sentence about luck favouring the prepared traveller.

archetype.simple: A first or typical model that later characters or stories copy.
archetype.detailed: A recurring pattern: the wise mentor, the trickster, or the journey home can be an archetype readers recognise across many texts.
archetype.example: The lonely lighthouse keeper fits the archetype of the isolated watcher.
archetype.basic: The lonely lighthouse keeper fits the typical model of the isolated watcher.

aristocracy.simple: A small upper class that holds titles, wealth, or inherited power.
aristocracy.detailed: Rule or social rank based on noble families rather than equal votes; HASS texts contrast aristocracy with democracy and ordinary citizens.
aristocracy.example: The novel shows how the local aristocracy tried to block the new public school.
aristocracy.basic: The novel shows how the titled upper class tried to block the new public school.

asylum.simple: Protection given to a person who is in danger if they go home.
asylum.detailed: Safe refuge granted by a country or institution: people may seek asylum from war or persecution, which HASS discusses as a human-rights issue.
asylum.example: The family applied for asylum after their village became too dangerous to stay in.
asylum.basic: The family applied for safe protection after their village became too dangerous to stay in.

atrocity.simple: An extremely cruel and shocking act, especially in war or persecution.
atrocity.detailed: A grave crime against people: massacre, torture, or organised cruelty that HASS and news writing name so the harm is not hidden in soft words.
atrocity.example: The museum exhibit does not hide the atrocity committed in the prison camp.
atrocity.basic: The museum exhibit does not hide the extremely cruel act committed in the prison camp.

audacity.simple: Boldness that can be brave, or so bold that it feels rude.
audacity.detailed: Daring that crosses a line: audacity can win a rescue, or it can mean cheek that shocks a community; tone tells you which.
audacity.example: It took real audacity to tell the mayor the flood maps were out of date.
audacity.basic: It took real boldness to tell the mayor the flood maps were out of date.

austerity.simple: A policy or lifestyle of strict saving and very few comforts.
austerity.detailed: Harsh simplicity, often in government budgets: austerity cuts spending, which can lower debt but also reduce services people rely on.
austerity.example: Years of austerity closed the only public swimming lessons in the shire.
austerity.basic: Years of strict saving closed the only public swimming lessons in the shire.

autocracy.simple: A system in which one person holds almost all political power.
autocracy.detailed: Rule by a single uncontrolled leader: an autocracy allows little real opposition, unlike a democracy with shared checks.
autocracy.example: The novel warns how quickly a frightened city can slide into autocracy.
autocracy.basic: The novel warns how quickly a frightened city can slide into one-person rule.

axiom.simple: A statement accepted as a starting truth that other ideas can build on.
axiom.detailed: A basic principle taken as given: in maths or argument an axiom is not proved in the moment, so you should still ask whether it is fair.
axiom.example: One axiom of fair testing is that only one variable should change at a time.
axiom.basic: One starting rule of fair testing is that only one variable should change at a time.

bastion.simple: A stronghold of a belief, group, or place that people try to defend.
bastion.detailed: Originally a fortress wall; now often a metaphor for an institution or town that holds out for a value, for better or worse.
bastion.example: The little library became a bastion of free reading after the book bans began.
bastion.basic: The little library became a stronghold of free reading after the book bans began.

belligerence.simple: An aggressive, ready-to-fight attitude in words or actions.
belligerence.detailed: Hostile combativeness: belligerence in a debate or between countries turns disagreement into attack and makes peace harder.
belligerence.example: His belligerence in the debate lost him marks even when his facts were sound.
belligerence.basic: His aggressive, ready-to-fight manner in the debate lost him marks even when his facts were sound.

brevity.simple: The quality of being short and using no extra words.
brevity.detailed: Concise length: brevity in a summary or speech is valued when every sentence still carries the needed meaning.
brevity.example: The judge praised the brevity of her closing statement: one page, no waffle.
brevity.basic: The judge praised how short and clear her closing statement was: one page, no waffle.

catharsis.simple: A strong release of feeling that leaves you calmer afterwards.
catharsis.detailed: An emotional clearing, often after a tragic or intense story: readers may feel catharsis when pent-up pity or fear is finally let out.
catharsis.example: The last scene offers catharsis after chapters of unspoken grief.
catharsis.basic: The last scene offers a strong release of feeling after chapters of unspoken grief.

caucus.simple: A private meeting of people from the same party or group to plan a decision.
caucus.detailed: A closed political or organisational huddle: a caucus chooses candidates or tactics before the public vote, which HASS treats as part of party process.
caucus.example: The party held a late-night caucus to decide who would speak against the bill.
caucus.basic: The party held a late-night private meeting to decide who would speak against the bill.

censure.simple: Strong official criticism that says someone's action was wrong.
censure.detailed: Formal blame, often from a parliament, board, or community: censure names the fault without always adding a legal punishment.
censure.example: The board issued a censure after the coach hid the injury report.
censure.basic: The board issued a strong official criticism after the coach hid the injury report.

chasm.simple: A deep gap in the ground, or a huge divide between people or ideas.
chasm.detailed: A wide split: physically a gorge, and figuratively a chasm of misunderstanding that argument or story must try to cross.
chasm.example: A chasm of distrust opened between the two towns after the water deal failed.
chasm.basic: A huge gap of distrust opened between the two towns after the water deal failed.

clemency.simple: Mercy shown by someone who has the power to punish.
clemency.detailed: Leniency from a judge, ruler, or school leader: clemency reduces a penalty because compassion or fairness outweighs strictness.
clemency.example: The principal showed clemency and replaced suspension with community service.
clemency.basic: The principal showed mercy and replaced suspension with community service.

coercion.simple: Forcing someone to act by using threats or pressure.
coercion.detailed: Unfree influence: coercion removes real choice, so a 'yes' given under coercion is not a fair agreement in law or ethics.
coercion.example: A confession written under coercion should not be treated as free evidence.
coercion.basic: A confession written under threats and pressure should not be treated as free evidence.

collusion.simple: A secret agreement to cheat or break the rules together.
collusion.detailed: Hidden cooperation for a dishonest aim: collusion in a test, a market, or a vote undermines fairness because the public cannot see the deal.
collusion.example: Markers suspected collusion when two papers used the same invented quotation.
collusion.basic: Markers suspected a secret cheating agreement when two papers used the same invented quotation.

compendium.simple: A short book or collection that gathers the main facts in one place.
compendium.detailed: A compact reference: a compendium of rules, stories, or species saves a reader from hunting through many scattered sources.
compendium.example: The teacher handed out a compendium of the ten most useful graph types.
compendium.basic: The teacher handed out a short collection of the ten most useful graph types.

complicity.simple: The state of being involved in a wrong act, even if you did not start it.
complicity.detailed: Shared blame: silence, help, or looking away can create complicity, which HASS and argument writing treat as a moral question.
complicity.example: The novel asks whether silence about the stolen wages is a kind of complicity.
complicity.basic: The novel asks whether silence about the stolen wages is a kind of shared blame.

connotation.simple: The extra feeling or idea a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning.
connotation.detailed: The shade a word carries: 'home' and 'house' can name the same building, but their connotations of warmth are different.
connotation.example: 'Slim' and 'skinny' can describe the same body, but the connotation of each word is different.
connotation.basic: 'Slim' and 'skinny' can describe the same body, but the extra feeling of each word is different.

constellation.simple: A named group of stars, or a group of related things seen together.
constellation.detailed: In science, a pattern of stars such as the Southern Cross; in wider writing, a constellation of clues or events that form one picture.
constellation.example: The class used the Southern Cross, a southern constellation, to find south at camp.
constellation.basic: The class used the Southern Cross, a named group of stars, to find south at camp.

consternation.simple: Sudden shocked worry when something unexpected goes wrong.
consternation.detailed: Dismayed alarm: consternation fills a room when a plan collapses or a secret is revealed, mixing surprise with distress.
consternation.example: There was consternation when the excursion buses were cancelled an hour before departure.
consternation.basic: There was shocked worry when the excursion buses were cancelled an hour before departure.

contingency.simple: A possible future event you plan for even if it may never happen.
contingency.detailed: A backup situation: good inquiry and civic planning include a contingency for rain, power loss, or missing data.
contingency.example: Our contingency plan is to move the fair indoors if the southerly arrives.
contingency.basic: Our backup plan is to move the fair indoors if the southerly arrives.

conundrum.simple: A puzzling problem that is hard to solve because every choice has a cost.
conundrum.detailed: A brain-twisting difficulty: a conundrum may be a riddle, or a real dilemma such as saving money versus saving a habitat.
conundrum.example: The class faced a conundrum: cheaper paper or paper that could be recycled locally.
conundrum.basic: The class faced a hard puzzle: cheaper paper or paper that could be recycled locally.

credence.simple: Belief that a claim or report deserves to be trusted.
credence.detailed: The weight of acceptance you give evidence: a second source can lend credence to a story, or a contradiction can remove credence.
credence.example: A second witness lent credence to the claim that the crossing lights had failed.
credence.basic: A second witness made the claim that the crossing lights had failed more believable.

culmination.simple: The final high point after a long build-up of work or events.
culmination.detailed: The peak that earlier steps have been leading towards: a concert, a verdict, or a last chapter can be the culmination of months of effort.
culmination.example: The science fair was the culmination of a term's work on water quality.
culmination.basic: The science fair was the final high point of a term's work on water quality.

cynicism.simple: The habit of doubting that people or promises are sincere.
cynicism.detailed: A distrustful outlook that expects selfish motives; it can protect you from slogans, but heavy cynicism can also dismiss real kindness.
cynicism.example: Years of broken promises bred cynicism about every new 'green' slogan.
cynicism.basic: Years of broken promises bred distrust about every new 'green' slogan.

dearth.simple: A serious shortage of something that is needed.
dearth.detailed: Too little of a resource, skill, or evidence: a dearth of rainfall, mentors, or reliable sources makes the next step harder.
dearth.example: There is a dearth of shade along the new bike path in midsummer.
dearth.basic: There is a serious shortage of shade along the new bike path in midsummer.

decorum.simple: Calm, polite behaviour that fits a formal or serious occasion.
decorum.detailed: Proper manners in a setting: courtroom, assembly, or ceremony decorum keeps respect visible, even when people disagree.
decorum.example: The speaker asked for decorum so both sides could finish without shouting.
decorum.basic: The speaker asked for calm, polite behaviour so both sides could finish without shouting.

deference.simple: Respectful yielding to someone because of their role, age, or knowledge.
deference.detailed: Courteous submission: students may show deference to an elder's story, but blind deference can also stop a needed question.
deference.example: In deference to the elder's request, the class waited before photographing the site.
deference.basic: Out of respect for the elder's request, the class waited before photographing the site.

demeanour.simple: The way a person looks, speaks, and carries themselves.
demeanour.detailed: Outward manner: a calm demeanour can hide fear, and a restless demeanour can reveal it; readers watch this as character evidence.
demeanour.example: His calm demeanour at the microphone did not match the shaking notes in his hand.
demeanour.basic: His calm outward manner at the microphone did not match the shaking notes in his hand.

denouement.simple: The closing part of a story where the mystery or problem is finally cleared up.
denouement.detailed: The untying of the plot after the climax: secrets are explained, and readers see how the conflict is resolved or left open on purpose.
denouement.example: In the denouement we learn who moved the boundary fence, and why nobody spoke.
denouement.basic: In the closing part of the story we learn who moved the boundary fence, and why nobody spoke.

despotism.simple: Cruel, unchecked rule by a leader who will not share power.
despotism.detailed: Tyrannical government: despotism crushes opposition and treats the state as one person's property, the opposite of accountable democracy.
despotism.example: The history unit contrasts parliamentary checks with unchecked despotism.
despotism.basic: The history unit contrasts parliamentary checks with cruel, unchecked one-person rule.

deterrent.simple: Something that discourages a person from doing a harmful or risky act.
deterrent.detailed: A warning cost or threat designed to prevent behaviour: a fine, a fence, or public shame can act as a deterrent if people believe it will apply.
deterrent.example: A visible ranger presence is a stronger deterrent than a faded 'no dumping' sign.
deterrent.basic: A visible ranger presence discourages dumping more than a faded sign does.

dexterity.simple: Skilful, precise use of the hands, or mental quickness in a tricky task.
